The main building at Chicago’s Ford City Mall will shut down for good — by court order — at noon on Monday, ending a yearslong legal struggle between the city and the property’s owner.

The vast indoor mall had a six-decade run as a top retail destination and gathering place for the Southwest Side’s West Lawn community, but a growing number of empty stores and unsafe conditions led city officials to file a lawsuit and force its closure.

Most of the few stores that remained inside have already closed. Outdoor tenants in the property’s North Mall and on other nearby lots, including Planet Fitness, IHOP and the AMC Ford City 14 movie theaters, were not targeted by the city and all remain open for business.

The future of the almost empty mall at 7601 S. Cicero Ave. remains in limbo. An industrial developer has proposed tearing it down and building several warehouses on the site. But North Mall store owners worry demolition could disrupt their water supply, and neighborhood advocates want to preserve the land as a community hub, with housing, more outdoor retail and green space.

“I’m OK with the (indoor) mall going away. Things get torn down and rebuilt all the time,” said Adolfo Castrejon, president and founder of the West Lawn Conservation Club. “But the Southwest Side can’t handle more industry. You can go down 65th Street in (suburban) Bedford Park, and it’s endless warehouses and manufacturing, and a lot of people have been asking for more green space.”

The few retailers left inside the mall, including anchor tenant JCPenney, fought to stay open, telling a Cook County judge this spring that a quick shutdown was unnecessary and wouldn’t leave enough time to wind down their businesses in an orderly manner.

But Greg Janes, assistant corporation counsel for the city, told the court that conditions were dangerous to shoppers. He noted in court filings the mall’s often malfunctioning fire suppression system and “huge water leaks, burst sprinkler heads, and blown booster pumps,” as well as “open wiring, dirty conditions, and poor lighting.”

Judge Leonard Murray ultimately sided with the city, issuing in May an order to permanently shutter the indoor mall at noon on Monday, June 22.

“Despite our best efforts to remain at Ford City Mall, JCPenney will close this location to the public by June 21, 2026, as a result of the city of Chicago’s motion to vacate the property due to safety concerns not addressed by the landlord,” a JCPenney spokesperson said last week. “We are actively exploring opportunities for a new store location in the surrounding Chicago area.”

A spokesperson for clothing and footwear store DTLR said its Ford City location was already closed.

Ford City Mall, a manufacturing site for B-29 bombers during World War II, opened in 1965 and for generations of Chicagoans was a popular and vibrant shopping destination. It had more than 100 stores during its heyday, but the rise of online retail left long stretches of the indoor mall entirely vacant. New York-based Namdar Realty Group, an investor known for buying up distressed retail, bought it for about $16 million in 2019.

“Prior to its decline, there were a lot of seasonal events including at Christmas time with Santa and his elves,” said Leonardo Rojas-Banda, a lawyer and lifelong West Lawn resident. “It was always the community’s place to hang out. There were also a lot of restaurants back in the day, and that helped make it an economic hub. I had a lot of friends who had jobs at the mall.”

Kurv Industrial, a national developer of distribution and logistics buildings, put forward a plan last summer to replace the mall with warehouses. Ald. Derrick Curtis, 18th, whose ward includes Ford City Mall, has said he supports the site’s redevelopment.

That proposal would need to overcome opposition from neighborhood groups such as Castrejon’s West Lawn Conservation Club and South West Area Neighbors. It also needs approvals from the Chicago Plan Commission and the full City Council.

North Mall tenants say they still worry shutting down or demolishing the main mall could affect their water supply, given that all the buildings use the same system.

“I asked (the court) if closing the (main mall) would affect our fire suppression water service and received mixed responses,” said Albert Barr, facilities director for Planet Fitness. “To date we’re being told that the water supply for the fire suppression will remain in effect. We’ve seen nothing in writing to assure us that will happen, and I’ve sent a couple of requests to the landlord asking for that assurance but haven’t received any confirmation.”

Namdar Realty Group did not return a message seeking comment.

Kristen Cabanban, a spokesperson for the city’s Law Department, said North Mall tenants should be able to operate normally.

“Namdar will continue to own the North Mall and will need to provide water and fire protection after the sale and demolition of the main mall,” she said.

Castrejon said the neighborhood groups have already held several well-attended meetings about replacing the mall, and most participants preferred a mix of residences, a public park, an open-air mall and perhaps a small museum commemorating the site’s role in World War II.

“The alderman and the city will feel pressure to put something there, but I think we have to do our due diligence,” he said. “We’re going to continue holding meetings, gather up these voices and come up with a proposal.”

Rojas-Banda said he didn’t favor Kurv’s plan for more warehouses.

“I’m open to anything as long as it serves the community,” he said.
